subject: organic-chemistry-1
question: A hypothetical study compound consists of an unbranched 12-carbon hydrocarbon chain bearing a single terminal hydroxyl group. Which prediction about its behavior in water is best supported?

options.text: It will be freely miscible, because long carbon chains create strong dipole–dipole attractions to water
It will be freely miscible, because a single hydroxyl group hydrogen bonds strongly enough to carry the molecule into solution
It will be poorly soluble, because the large nonpolar chain outweighs one polar hydroxyl group
It will dissolve as an ionic solution, because hydroxyl groups release hydrogen ions in water

explanation:
Alcohol solubility falls sharply as the carbon-to-hydroxyl ratio rises: methanol, ethanol, and 1-propanol are miscible with water, 1-butanol is only partly soluble, and alcohols of five or more carbons per hydroxyl are increasingly insoluble. At a ratio of 12 / 1 = 12 carbons per hydroxyl, the hydrophobic surface that water must reorganize around dwarfs the hydrogen-bonding contribution of one —OH. Choice D also fails because alcohols have pKa near 16 and do not measurably ionize at physiological pH.

ELI-10: Solubility is a competition between the polar part of a molecule, which water welcomes, and the nonpolar part, which forces water into an ordered cage that costs energy. A short alcohol like 1-propanol has 3 carbons for its one —OH and the polar end wins. Stretch the chain to 12 carbons for the same single —OH and the ratio is 12 / 1, so the nonpolar side dominates and the compound behaves more like an oil or a wax than like rubbing alcohol. The same logic explains why fatty acids need bile salts to disperse in the aqueous contents of the intestine.
